references.text: Jesus had just said to the sick man, "Stand up, take your mat and walk!" ([ref:Joh 5:8-9|John 5:8-9]). In verse 11, the man defends himself before the Jews by referring back to this command from the one who healed him.

The man born blind gives a similar answer when he is questioned: he points to the one who healed him as his authority ([ref:Joh 9:11|John 9:11]). Both healed men defend themselves by pointing to Jesus' words.
Also in the story of the man born blind, Jesus is accused of breaking the Sabbath through healing ([ref:Joh 9:14-16|John 9:14-16]), just as in the Sabbath controversy here in chapter 5.
The Jews' reaction to the man's answer is to ask who gave him this command ([ref:Joh 5:12-13|John 5:12-13]), showing that they were more concerned with the Sabbath violation than with the healing.

Nehemiah rebuked those who desecrated the Sabbath by carrying burdens ([ref:Neh 13:19|Nehemiah 13:19]). The Sabbath command not to carry burdens was the basis for the Jews' accusation against the healed man.

Jeremiah conveyed God's prohibition against carrying burdens on the Sabbath day ([ref:Jer 17:21-22|Jeremiah 17:21-22]). This is the Old Testament background for the accusation that the man carried his mat on the Sabbath.

Jesus later argues that if circumcision can be performed on the Sabbath, it should also be allowed to make a whole person well ([ref:Joh 7:23|John 7:23]). This continues the Sabbath controversy that begins in this passage.
